title: Filters in ASP.NET Core
description: Understand what filters are, the four built-in filter types, and how to create custom filters for authorization, actions, results, and exceptions.

data.text: Filters in ASP.NET Core are reusable pieces of code that run **before or after** specific stages of the MVC request pipeline. They help you centralize cross-cutting concerns — like logging, caching, authorization, and exception handling — so you do not have to repeat the same logic in every action method.

terms.definition: A class that runs code at a specific stage of the MVC pipeline.
The ordered sequence in which filters execute during a single request.
A requirement that applies across many parts of an app, such as logging or authorization.
Code that runs on every request before routing; unlike filters, it cannot target specific actions.

data.caption: How a request flows through the ASP.NET Core filter pipeline
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[HTTP Request] --> B[Middleware]
    B --> C[Routing]
    C --> D[Authorization Filters]
    D --> E[Action Filters]
    E --> F[Action Method]
    F --> G[Result Filters]
    G --> H[Response]
    I[Exception Filters] -.->|on error| H

data.text: A common question is: **when should I use middleware and when should I use a filter?** The table below summarizes the key differences.

data.title: Quick Rule of Thumb
data.text: Use middleware for concerns that apply to all requests. Use filters when you need access to MVC-specific context or want to target only certain actions.
ASP.NET Core provides four built-in filter types, each designed for a specific stage of the request pipeline:

rows: Before and after the action method
Before and after the action result

data.text: Authorization filters run **first** in the pipeline. They determine whether a request is allowed to proceed. If an authorization filter sets a result — for example, a 403 Forbidden — the action method never runs.

data.title: Custom Authorization Filter
data.content: Block non-HTTPS requests by returning 403 Forbidden.

data.title: Exercise: Block HTTP Requests
data.description: Create an authorization filter called RequireHttpsAttribute that returns a 403 Forbidden status when the incoming request is not HTTPS. Apply it to a controller action and verify it blocks non-HTTPS traffic.
data.expectedOutcome: When you browse to the action over HTTP, you see a 403 error. Over HTTPS, the action executes normally.

data.text: Action filters run immediately before and after an action method executes. They are the most commonly used filter type for adding logic around the action's execution — for example, measuring execution time or validating input state.

data.title: Synchronous Action Filter
data.content: Measure how long an action method takes to run using a Stopwatch.

data.title: Asynchronous Action Filter
data.content: The same Stopwatch logic written with the async interface.

cards.title: IActionFilter (Sync)
cards.description: Two separate methods: OnActionExecuting and OnActionExecuted.
pros: Easy to add logic before and after

cards.title: IAsyncActionFilter
cards.description: Single method with an ActionExecutionDelegate to invoke the next stage.
pros: Single method keeps before/after logic together

data.text: Result filters run before and after the action result is processed. Use them to modify the response — for example, changing the view name or adding a header — before it is sent to the client.

data.title: Result Filter: Change the Rendered View
data.content: Swap the view rendered by an action method without modifying the action itself.

data.title: Async Result Filter
data.content: The same view-swapping logic written with the async interface.

data.text: Exception filters catch unhandled exceptions from action methods. They are a clean alternative to wrapping every action in a try/catch block. Because exception filters run after the action method, they cannot catch exceptions from authorization or action filters.

data.title: Limitation
data.text: Exception filters only catch exceptions thrown by the action method itself, not by other filters. Use them for logging or friendly error pages, not for critical error recovery.

data.title: Exception Filter: Friendly Error Page
data.content: Capture exceptions and return a friendly error view with the exception message.

data.text: Sometimes you want the same filter class to act as both an action filter and a result filter. The easiest way to achieve this is to inherit from **ActionFilterAttribute**, which implements both IActionFilter and IResultFilter.

data.title: Hybrid Filter: Measure Time and Change View
data.content: A single filter that starts a timer before the action and renders a view with the elapsed time after the result.

items.text: Create a class that inherits from Attribute and implements the desired filter interface.
Override the appropriate methods (OnActionExecuting, OnException, etc.).
Apply the filter as an attribute on a controller or action method.
Run the app and verify the filter behavior.
Choose the async interface when the filter needs to perform I/O.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Filters run at specific stages of the MVC request pipeline.
There are four filter types: Authorization, Action, Result, and Exception.
Each filter type has a synchronous and an asynchronous interface.
Hybrid filters combine action and result behavior in a single class by inheriting ActionFilterAttribute.
Use filters for MVC-specific concerns; use middleware for global concerns.
data.takeaway: Next, you will learn how to inject services into filters, register them globally, and control their execution order.
